method: The canvas is cut as the finished front face plus the bar depth and fold-under on every side, so both cut dimensions grow by twice the sum of those two allowances; the same rule is solved backwards to give the largest face that a canvas of known cut size can cover. The bar depth becomes the visible wrap band on each side of a gallery wrap, while the fold-under is turned to the back and never shows, so an image that runs around the edge has to extend past the face by at least the bar depth. Measurements are entered in inches or centimetres and converted with the exact 2.54 centimetre inch; the arithmetic is linear, so the geometry is the same in either unit, and areas are reported in square inches and square feet or square centimetres and square metres. Values are refused outside 1 to 240 inches (2.5 to 600 centimetres) for the face size, 1 to 400 inches (2.5 to 1000 centimetres) for a canvas entered in fit mode, 0.25 to 4 inches (0.6 to 10 centimetres) for the bar depth and 0 to 12 inches (0 to 30 centimetres) for the fold-under, and a canvas that is not wider and taller than twice the bar depth plus fold-under is refused in fit mode. The page is pure arithmetic: it does not judge whether a bar profile suits a canvas size, assess stretcher strength, allow for squaring a stretched edge or model canvas weave direction, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: A stretched canvas needs canvas on every side for the bar depth plus enough to turn under and staple to the back, so the cut size is the face size plus twice the bar depth and fold-under.
Stretcher bar depth is the profile thickness, and on a gallery wrap the image continues across that depth so the sides show the image rather than bare canvas.
One inch is exactly 2.54 centimetres, so converting a measurement between the two units leaves the geometry of the cut unchanged.
